Al-Muizz Street is one of Cairo’s most famous historic streets, dating back to the Fatimid era. It is known for its beautiful Islamic architecture, historic mosques, schools, houses, and traditional markets. Today, it is a major cultural and tourist attraction in Historic Cairo.

attributes.Description: The Hanging Church is one of Cairo’s most famous Coptic landmarks. Built above the remains of Babylon Fortress, it is known for its icons, wooden details, and decorated marble pulpit.
The Mosque of Amr Ibn Al-As is the oldest surviving mosque in Egypt and Africa. It is closely associated with the founding of Fustat and represents an important site in early Islamic architecture.
Qaitbay Citadel is a prominent Mamluk fortress on Alexandria’s Mediterranean coast. Built over the site of the ancient Lighthouse of Alexandria, it served as a major coastal defense.
Bab al-Nasr is one of the northern gates of Fatimid Cairo. Built in the 11th century as part of the city’s fortifications, it is distinguished by its stone towers and defensive decoration.
Bab al-Futuh is a historic gate of Fatimid Cairo, distinguished by its rounded towers and defensive architecture. It stands at the northern entrance of Al-Muizz Street in historic Cairo.

attributes.English_Name: Mosque and Madrasa of Sultan Hasan
attributes.Description: The Mosque and Madrasa of Sultan Hasan is one of Cairo’s greatest Mamluk monuments. It features a central courtyard, four iwans, religious schools, and richly carved stone and marble decoration.
Al-Rifa’i Mosque is a prominent architectural landmark in Salah Al-Din Square. It combines elaborate Islamic decoration with royal burial chambers and stands opposite Sultan Hasan Mosque.
Shali Fortress is a historic mud-brick settlement in Siwa Oasis, built from traditional kershef and clay. Its ruins offer distinctive views over the palm-filled oasis.
The Oracle Temple at Siwa stands on the Aghurmi hill and was associated with the worship of Amun. It is famous for the tradition of Alexander the Great consulting its oracle.
The Mountain of the Dead is a large rock-cut cemetery in Siwa, containing tombs carved into the hillside with decorations and inscriptions revealing the area’s funerary history.
Cleopatra’s Spring is a famous natural spring in Siwa Oasis, surrounded by palm trees and desert scenery, offering one of the oasis’s most memorable natural experiences.
Siwa’s salt lakes combine highly saline water with dramatic desert scenery. They are known for clear water, natural buoyancy, and striking opportunities for photography.
Qasr Al-Farafra is a historic settlement in Farafra Oasis, characterized by traditional mud-brick buildings and an old urban layout reflecting oasis life over centuries.
Badr Museum in Farafra presents artworks inspired by desert landscapes and oasis life, offering a distinctive cultural experience beyond conventional museums.
Agabat Valley is a spectacular desert landscape surrounded by rock formations and golden dunes, making it ideal for adventure, camping, and photography.
Crystal Mountain is a distinctive geological formation in Egypt’s Western Desert, where quartz crystals appear among the rocks, making it a memorable stop on desert trips.
Magic Lake in Fayoum is a peaceful desert lake known for reflections of the sky and surrounding landscape, especially beautiful at sunset and under the night sky.
Djara Cave is a rare natural cave in the Western Desert, featuring rock formations and crystalline deposits shaped over thousands of years. It attracts adventure and geology enthusiasts.
Wadi Al-Hitan is a remarkable natural and fossil site containing ancient whale remains, providing unique evidence of whale evolution and major environmental changes in Egypt.
Tuna El-Gebel is an archaeological area containing tombs, catacombs, and funerary structures associated with ancient Hermopolis and its religious history.
The Beni Hasan Tombs are rock-cut tombs decorated with colorful scenes depicting daily life, sports, crafts, and society in ancient Egypt.
Tell El-Amarna contains the remains of Akhenaten’s ancient capital and offers insight into the Amarna Period and its major religious and artistic transformation.
El-Kab is an ancient settlement containing tombs, inscriptions, temples, and defensive remains, offering insight into the political and religious history of Upper Egypt.
Deir el-Medina was home to the artisans who built and decorated royal tombs. Its small, richly painted tombs provide an intimate view of ancient Egyptian daily life.
The Temple of Esna is a Ptolemaic-Roman temple in the city of Esna, famous for its decorated hypostyle hall, astronomical imagery, and hieroglyphic inscriptions.
Deir al-Surian is one of Wadi El-Natrun’s historic monasteries, containing churches, manuscripts, and monastic heritage reflecting centuries of Coptic religious life.
The Abu Simbel Temples are masterpieces of ancient Egyptian architecture, carved into the rock by Ramesses II and featuring monumental temples dedicated to him and Queen Nefertari.
Karnak is Egypt’s largest ancient religious complex, containing halls, columns, obelisks, and temples that demonstrate the evolution of Egyptian sacred architecture over centuries.
Luxor Temple is a major riverside architectural landmark, incorporating additions by several rulers and known for its pylon, colossal statues, colonnade, and Opet Festival scenes.
The Valley of the Kings is Egypt’s most famous royal necropolis, containing more than sixty rock-cut tombs decorated with funerary texts and imagery.
The Valley of the Queens is a royal necropolis containing tombs of queens and princes from the New Kingdom, especially famous for Nefertari’s richly decorated tomb.
Hatshepsut’s temple at Deir el-Bahari is an architectural masterpiece of rising terraces against the cliffs, featuring famous scenes of the Punt expedition and royal rituals.
The Ramesseum is the mortuary temple of Ramesses II, preserving halls, columns, colossal statues, and reliefs depicting the Battle of Kadesh and royal rituals.
Medinet Habu is the mortuary temple of Ramesses III, notable for its excellent preservation and walls decorated with battle scenes, rituals, and historical inscriptions.
The Tomb of Ramesses VI features long decorated corridors, funerary texts, and astronomical ceilings, offering an outstanding example of New Kingdom funerary art.
Dendera is one of Egypt’s best-preserved temples, famous for its monumental Hathor-headed columns, decorated ceilings, and remarkable astronomical scenes.
Edfu Temple is one of the most complete ancient Egyptian temples, featuring a monumental pylon, courtyard, columned halls, and a sanctuary dedicated to Horus.
Kom Ombo is a unique double temple dedicated to Sobek and Horus, known for its symmetrical design, religious scenes, calendars, and depictions linked to ancient medicine.
Philae is a remarkable Ptolemaic-Roman complex on Agilkia Island, featuring the Temple of Isis, Trajan’s Kiosk, and Temple of Hathor, relocated to save it from flooding.
The Unfinished Obelisk demonstrates ancient Egyptian granite-working techniques. Still lying in its quarry, it reveals the stages involved in producing monumental obelisks.
Kalabsha Temple is one of Nubia’s notable monuments, combining Egyptian, Greek, and Roman influences. It was relocated as part of the campaign to save Nubian heritage.
Sehel Island contains numerous rock inscriptions, including the famous Famine Stela, which tells the story of seven years of drought during the reign of Djoser.
The Temple of Seti I at Abydos is one of Egypt’s finest temples, famous for detailed reliefs, the Abydos King List, and religious scenes associated with Osiris.
The Osireion is a mysterious structure associated with the cult of Osiris at Abydos, distinguished by massive stone blocks, sunken chambers, and unusual architecture.

attributes.English_Name: Temple of Seti I at Qurna
attributes.Description: Seti I’s temple at Qurna is a New Kingdom mortuary temple on Luxor’s west bank, containing religious reliefs and important examples of royal architecture.
Kom El-Dikka is a Roman-Byzantine archaeological site containing a theater, baths, mosaics, and lecture halls, offering a detailed picture of ancient urban life.
The Catacombs of Kom El-Shoqafa are a unique Roman necropolis blending Egyptian, Greek, and Roman traditions through underground chambers and funerary decoration.
Pompey’s Pillar is a massive Roman granite column standing beside the remains of the Serapeum and is one of ancient Alexandria’s best-known surviving monuments.
Alexandria’s Roman Theater forms part of Kom El-Dikka and is known for its marble seating, mosaics, and layout reflecting the cultural life of ancient Alexandria.
The Mosque of Muhammad Ali inside Cairo Citadel is a major landmark of modern Egyptian architecture, famous for its marble surfaces, domes, tall minarets, and copper clock tower.
Al-Azhar Mosque is one of Cairo’s oldest and most important mosques and a major center of Islamic scholarship, incorporating architectural elements from several historical periods.
Al-Hakim Mosque is a major monument of Fatimid Cairo, distinguished by its monumental façade, minarets, and long history of restoration and reuse.
Bayt Al-Sinnari is a historic Ottoman-era house distinguished by its traditional interior layout and courtyard, with strong connections to Cairo’s cultural and intellectual history.
Rosetta’s historic houses showcase Egyptian Ottoman-era domestic architecture, characterized by mashrabiyas, brick façades, and distinctive interior spatial arrangements.
Saint Catherine’s Monastery is one of the world’s oldest continuously functioning Christian monasteries, located at Mount Sinai and preserving churches, manuscripts, and exceptional artworks.

A specialized museum dedicated to Egypt and Alexandria during the Greek and Roman periods, displaying statues, mosaics, jewelry, and architectural elements reflecting the interaction of Egyptian and classical cultures.
Manial Palace is a unique architectural complex combining Islamic, Ottoman, Persian, and Andalusian influences, displaying the collections and royal lifestyle of Prince Muhammad Ali.
Housed in a historic palace, the museum displays luxurious jewelry and possessions of Egypt’s Muhammad Ali dynasty alongside distinctive architectural and decorative details.
Housed in an Italianate historic palace, the museum presents Alexandria and Egypt from prehistory to modern times, including underwater antiquities and Coptic and Islamic collections.
A distinguished museum on Luxor’s Corniche displaying carefully selected artifacts from ancient Thebes, including statues, royal objects, and pieces associated with Luxor’s temples.
A specialized museum explaining ancient Egyptian mummification and burial practices through mummies, embalming tools, coffins, and funerary objects.
The Nubian Museum presents Nubian history and culture from prehistory to modern times and features architecture inspired by Nubian heritage and environment.
Located on Elephantine Island, the museum displays artifacts connected to Aswan and Nubian history, including temple objects, funerary finds, and everyday items.
A distinctive museum at Saqqara honoring architect Imhotep and displaying artifacts connected to Saqqara and the construction of Djoser’s Step Pyramid complex.
A museum presenting diverse aspects of Egyptian civilization while highlighting the heritage, environment, and cultural diversity of South Sinai and the Red Sea region.
The museum displays archaeological and artistic objects from different periods of Egyptian history, providing a cultural experience within a major Red Sea resort city.
Housed within historic Abdeen Palace, the museum displays royal collections, weapons, and documents while the palace itself reflects an important period of modern Egyptian history.
An art museum in Alexandria dedicated to Mahmoud Said, displaying works that represent the development of modern Egyptian painting and the spirit of Alexandria.
Shunet El-Zebib at Abydos is a massive mud-brick funerary enclosure from early Egyptian history, representing an important stage in the development of royal architecture.
The Red Monastery is a major Coptic monastery in Upper Egypt, known for its historic church and rich murals combining Egyptian, classical, and Christian influences.
The White Monastery is a historic Coptic complex distinguished by its monumental stone façade and unique church, representing an important example of Upper Egyptian religious architecture.
The Meir Tombs are rock-cut tombs of officials from Middle Egypt, featuring colorful scenes depicting daily life, agriculture, hunting, and funerary rituals.
Ashmunein contains the remains of ancient Hermopolis, with Egyptian, Greek, and Roman monuments connected to the worship of Thoth and the city’s religious history.

attributes.Description: Zawyet Sultan is a lesser-known archaeological area containing the remains of a stepped pyramid, tombs, and ancient structures away from Egypt’s busiest tourist sites.
Al-Qasr is a historic village in Dakhla Oasis characterized by mud-brick buildings and narrow passages, reflecting the development of Islamic domestic architecture in the oases.
Deir El-Hagar is a small Roman temple in Dakhla Oasis dedicated to Amun and Thoth, distinguished by preserved reliefs and its peaceful desert setting.
Bagawat is one of Egypt’s oldest and most important Christian necropolises, containing mud-brick tombs and domed chapels with distinctive religious decoration.
Dush is an isolated Roman archaeological site in Kharga Oasis, combining a temple, defensive structures, and settlement remains within a striking desert environment.
Ain Umm Dabadib is a remote desert landscape known for springs and mountain scenery, combining water and desert environments far from major cities.
Wadi El-Wishwashi is a hidden desert oasis near Nuweiba, known for a natural pool surrounded by rocks and offering a distinctive adventure experience.
Ain Khudra is a small oasis in the Sinai desert, featuring a water source, vegetation, and mountain scenery, making it a peaceful stop on desert safaris.
Wadi El-Gemal is a vast protected area combining mountains, desert, and sea, with rock art, Ptolemaic and Roman remains, and diverse natural landscapes.
The Monastery of St. Simeon is a major historic monastery in Aswan, preserving churches and monastic structures built from stone and mud brick across a distinctive desert landscape.
Qasr El-Ghuweita is a fortified archaeological site in Kharga Oasis containing a temple and remains from different periods, with distinctive desert views and architecture.
